newsitem.title: USA: Blair cites girl's plea in N. Ireland peace vow.
newsitem.headline: Blair cites girl's plea in N. Ireland peace vow.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair promised on Sunday to work for an end to violence in Northern Ireland for the sake of a young girl who told him she had known only one year of peace in her life.

Interviewed by ABC Television, Blair said people in the British-ruled province were yearning for restoration of the 17-month ceasefire that the IRA shattered in February 1996 with a series of bomb attacks on the British mainland.

"We've got the chance now for people in Northern Ireland. They're desperate for peace. When there was peace for that year or more and President Clinton came and visited Northern Ireland, I can't tell you what it meant to families and people on the streets of Northern Ireland," he said.
"I got a letter from a little girl just a couple of days ago, who just said to me: 'Do whatever you can for peace in Northern Ireland. I've only had one year of peace in my life'," Blair said.

He again urged the outlawed Irish Republican Army to declare an unequivocal ceasefire in its camapign to oust Britain from Northern Ireland in order to win a seat at peace talks for its political allies, Sinn Fein.
Blair vowed that multi-party peace talks being chaired by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell would go on, with or without Sinn Fein.

"If Sinn Fein don't come into this, they can't hold it to ransom. They can't sit there and say 'we're not going to let anyone else talk about a lasting settlement in Northern Ireland because we won't'," Blair said.
"If they don't face up to their responibility, we as the British government have got to face up to ours and take that process forward," he added.

He praised U.S. President Bill Clinton for his strong support and said he did not expect the U.S. administration would grant any fresh visa request by Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams in the light of last week's IRA murder of two policemen.
"That is a matter for them, but I would have thought there was very little prospect of that happening while Sinn Fein continue to play with violence," Blair said.
Britain suspended contacts with Sinn Fein after the killings in the town of Lurgan, southeast of Belfast.

Officials disclosed during this weekend's summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations in Denver that the IRA carried out the killings shortly after Britain had privately told Sinn Fein it could join peace talks within six weeks of a written IRA ceasefire.
